title: Why $9.99 Works on Your Brain (Even When You Know the Trick)
description: One cent should not matter. Yet prices ending in .99 change what we buy, what we notice and even what we pay for a used car. Here is the brain glitch behind it, the experiments that proved it, and how to stop falling for it.
sources: Thomas, M. & Morwitz, V. (2005). Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition. Journal of Consumer Research.
Anderson, E. & Simester, D. (2003). Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments. Quantitative Marketing and Economics.
Lacetera, N., Pope, D. & Sydnor, J. (2012). Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market. American Economic Review.

beats.text: Look at this price. $9.99. Now be honest. Does it feel like ten dollars?
beats.say: Look at this price. Nine ninety-nine. Now be honest. Does it feel like ten dollars?

visual.prompt: a large paper price tag hanging on a string, centered in the frame, plain cream background, bold red border

beats.text: It doesn't. And that single missing cent is one of the most profitable tricks in the history of selling.

prompts: a single shiny copper penny lying on a green felt table, dramatic spotlight
an old brass cash register overflowing with paper money, glowing warm light

beats.text: Walk into any store and you will see it everywhere. Nineteen ninety-nine. Four ninety-nine. Ninety-nine cents.

prompts: a 1950s supermarket aisle with neat rows of colorful cans, wide view
a row of price tags on a shop shelf edge, close view, red and cream colors

beats.text: So why does it work? And why does it still work on you, even right now, when you already know it is a trick?

visual.prompt: a thoughtful man in a 1950s suit and hat scratching his head while looking at a shop window

beats.section: How your brain reads a price
beats.text: Chapter one. How your brain reads a price.

visual.text: How your brain reads a price

beats.section: How your brain reads a price
beats.text: Your brain is lazy in a very clever way. It reads numbers from left to right, and it decides fast.

visual.prompt: a stylized human brain made of gears and cogs inside a glass dome, mid-century illustration

beats.section: How your brain reads a price
beats.text: The first digit it sees becomes an anchor. Two ninety-nine starts with a two, so it gets filed as two dollars and something.

visual.prompt: a heavy iron ship anchor resting on a stack of coins, centered in the frame, side view

beats.section: How your brain reads a price
beats.text: But look at the real gap. Two ninety-nine is not close to two. It is one cent away from three.

chart.title: The real gap is one cent

beats.section: How your brain reads a price
beats.text: Researchers call this the left-digit effect. The digit on the left gets most of the attention, and the cents get almost none.

visual.prompt: a magnifying glass centered over a large printed number on cream paper

beats.text: Chapter two. The experiments.
In 2005, two marketing researchers, Manoj Thomas and Vicki Morwitz, showed that people judge a price ending in nine as noticeably cheaper, but mostly when the left digit changes.

prompts: a 1950s research laboratory with a scientist in a white coat holding a clipboard
two price cards on a table, one slightly lower than the other, clean studio light

beats.text: Going from three dollars to two ninety-nine feels like a real discount. Going from three sixty to three fifty-nine barely registers.
beats.say: Going from three dollars to two ninety-nine feels like a real discount. Going from three sixty to three fifty-nine barely registers.

visual.prompt: a shop clerk in a 1950s uniform replacing a price card on a display stand

beats.text: Then came a field test with real money. Economists Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester worked with a mail-order clothing catalog.

visual.prompt: a stack of vintage mail-order clothing catalogs on a wooden desk next to a pen

beats.text: They printed different versions of the same catalog, with the same dress at different prices. Thirty-four dollars, thirty-nine, and forty-four.

visual.prompt: a 1950s dress on a mannequin in a boutique window, elegant lighting

beats.text: The result sounds impossible. The thirty-nine dollar version sold more than the cheaper thirty-four dollar one.

visual.prompt: a shocked 1950s shop owner in an apron staring at a sales ledger, mouth open, centered

bubble.text: Wait… the pricier one sold MORE?!

beats.text: A higher price sold more. The nine at the end did not just look cheaper. It looked like a deal.

beats.section: It is not just price tags
beats.text: Chapter three. It is not just price tags.

beats.section: It is not just price tags
beats.text: The same glitch shows up in places with much bigger money. Take used cars.

visual.prompt: a shiny 1950s sedan parked on a used car lot with bunting flags

beats.section: It is not just price tags
beats.text: A study of millions of wholesale car sales found that prices drop sharply when the odometer crosses a round number, like ten thousand miles.

beats.section: It is not just price tags
beats.text: A car with seventy-nine thousand nine hundred miles is basically the same car as one with eighty thousand. But buyers pay noticeably more for it.

prompts: two identical vintage cars side by side in a showroom, symmetrical composition
a car salesman in a checked jacket shaking hands with a happy customer

beats.text: Chapter four. How to beat the trick.
Here is the good news. The fix is simple. Round every price up before you decide.

visual.prompt: a hand-held pencil writing a round number on a small notepad, cream paper

beats.text: Nine ninety-nine is ten. Forty-nine ninety-nine is fifty. Say the rounded number out loud, and the magic disappears.

visual.prompt: a vintage stage magician lifting an empty top hat, surprised expression, theatrical spotlight, centered

beats.text: And when a price ends in nine, ask one question. Is this actually cheap, or does it just look cheap?
Because the people who set that price already know how your brain reads it. Now you do too.
Why does every price end in ninety-nine?
Because your brain reads prices from left to right, and the first digit wins.
Two ninety-nine gets filed as two dollars. It is one cent from three.
In one real catalog test, a dress at thirty-nine dollars outsold the same dress at thirty-four.
A higher price sold more, just because it ended in nine.
So next time, round up. And remember exactly why every price ends in…
